What Is an EventEmitter? →

Emit, and Let Listeners React

Splitting 'a ticket was created' from 'here's everything that should happen next' — the service only has to announce the first.

The fix is to pull those two jobs apart. createTicket keeps exactly the one job it started with — insert the row — and adds a single new one: announce, once, that a ticket was created. It doesn't say who should react, how many things should happen, or what any of them involve. Something else entirely — three completely separate modules, one per channel — is listening for that announcement and reacts independently:

createTicket()
     │
     │ emit('ticket.created', ticket)
     ▼
 domain event
     │
     ├──▶ write a Notification row
     ├──▶ send a confirmation email
     └──▶ push a Socket.IO update

Each arrow on the right is a listener that exists in its own file, knows nothing about the other two, and can be added, removed, or rewritten without createTicket — or either of the other listeners — changing at all. This is the same shape CLAUDE.md's Architecture conventions describe: "listeners (email, in-app notifications, real-time push) are decoupled from the controllers that trigger them." The rest of this lesson builds exactly that — a shared way to announce an event (next topic), the four places this project announces one, and the three listener modules reacting to them.
